newsitem.title: USA: Dole calls for Clinton to release drug memo.
newsitem.headline: Dole calls for Clinton to release drug memo.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole demanded on Wednesday that President Bill Clinton make public an FBI report critical of the administration's drug policy.
Dole said the White House was using executive privilege to keep the report from the public.
"Mr. President, it is time to release this memo so that the American people can see how bad your drug policy has been over the past 44 months. We are going to demand its release," Dole said.
Dole made the demand of Clinton in a speech before a crowd of cheering students at Elizabethtown College in central Pennsylvania, a state critical in his uphill battle for the presidency.

In his only campaign event Wednesday, Dole raced through a laundry list of areas where he claimed Clinton had failed as president -- from raising taxes and thereby forcing both parents in a family to go to work, to doing so little in the war against drugs that teenage drug use doubled in 44 months.

He mocked the president for refusing to release his medical records, saying he had released his own, and he criticised Clinton for vetoing a Congressional ban on late- term abortions, an important issue in Pennsylvania with its 23 electorial votes.
The Keystone Poll, conducted for several news organisations in the state, showed Dole trailing Clinton by 16 points in Pennsylvania with 33 percent to the president's 49 percent.

"This election is about choosing an administration you can trust to fight a real war against crime and drugs, ... After years of success under Presidents Reagan and Bush, the Clinton administration came into office and threw it all away," Dole said.

"Their record is so bad that they don't want the story to get out," he added as he demanded that Clinton release a memo written by FBI director Louis Freeh 18 months ago that allegedly complained about the lack of any leadership to fight an influx of heroin and cocaine into the United States.
"Just yesterday, we learned that the White House is invoking executive privilege to keep that memo from seeing the light of day," he added.
There was no immediate reaction from the Clinton campaign.
Dole was scheduled to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu early Wednesday evening, according to Dole aides.
Nelson Warfield, Dole's spokesman, described the two men as old friends and said Dole wanted to show his support for Netanyahu.

The Dole camp set up the meeting with Netanyahu but did not attempt to arrange a similiar meeting with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, Warfield said, denying that any politics was involved in the decision.

By maintaining a light campaign load, Dole has been able to concentrate on preparing for the debate Sunday night in Hartford with Clinton, the first of two encounters that could sway millions of Americans in their decision as to who they should vote for.
Tennesssee Sen. Fred Thompson, a former actor, is playing the Clinton role in a series of make-believe debates Dole is conducting in preparation for the real event.
Warfield joked that the campaign had been considering using disgraced Clinton adviser Dick Morris as the Clinton stand-in "because he has been president for the last two years."
